nodes.label: Igehalkid dynasty
nodes.full: Founded by Igehalki, the dynasty consolidated Elam's highland-lowland dual kingship and cultivated marriage ties with the Kassite dynasty ruling Babylon — a period of relative peace and dynastic intermarriage that laid the economic and political foundation for the far more ambitious building and military programs of Igehalki's successors.
nodes.src: Igehalkid royal inscriptions, Susa; Kassite-Elamite marriage evidence in Babylonian and Elamite royal titulature.

nodes.label: King of Anshan and Susa
nodes.full: Middle Elamite kings formally styled themselves 'King of Anshan and Susa,' a dual title asserting rule over both the highland Fars plateau and the lowland Khuzestan capital — a titulature that made Elam's characteristic two-centre political geography an explicit, permanent part of royal legitimacy rather than an informal arrangement.
nodes.src: Middle Elamite royal titulature, attested across the Igehalkid and Shutrukid inscription corpus.

nodes.label: Wealth behind Chogha Zanbil
nodes.full: Building an entirely new ceremonial capital from scratch, complete with a monumental ziggurat, required agricultural surplus and organised labour on a scale only a kingdom controlling both Susa's fertile lowland and Anshan's highland resources could sustain — Untash-Napirisha's project doubled as a demonstration of exactly that combined economic capacity.
nodes.src: Roman Ghirshman, Chogha Zanbil excavations, on the site's construction scale and resource requirements.

nodes.label: Untash-Napirisha
nodes.full: Untash-Napirisha founded an entirely new religious capital, Dur-Untash, built around a massive ziggurat dedicated jointly to Susa's god Inshushinak and the highland god Napirisha — a deliberate architectural statement of religious unification between Elam's lowland and highland halves, married to a Kassite Babylonian princess as part of his dynasty's diplomatic strategy.
nodes.src: Untash-Napirisha's foundation inscriptions, Chogha Zanbil; Roman Ghirshman, Chogha Zanbil excavations (1951–62).

nodes.label: Ziggurat of Dur-Untash
nodes.full: Untash-Napirisha's ziggurat, dedicated jointly to Inshushinak of Susa and Napirisha of the highlands, survives today as the best-preserved ziggurat anywhere in the ancient Near East — its dual dedication a deliberate religious statement binding Elam's lowland and highland cults into a single, shared sacred architecture.
nodes.src: Chogha Zanbil excavations, Roman Ghirshman (1951–62); UNESCO World Heritage inscription (1979).

nodes.label: Ziggurat architecture
nodes.full: Built as a single unified structure rather than the accretive expansions typical of Mesopotamian ziggurats, Chogha Zanbil's five-stage tower survives today taller and more architecturally legible than any comparable Mesopotamian example — an engineering and artistic achievement recognised with UNESCO World Heritage status in 1979.
nodes.src: Chogha Zanbil excavations, Roman Ghirshman (1951–62); UNESCO World Heritage Site inscription (1979).

nodes.label: Ziggurat construction
nodes.full: Chogha Zanbil's ziggurat was built as baked and unbaked mudbrick in a single planned construction campaign, incorporating internal drainage to manage the region's seasonal rains — engineering choices that account for its unusually good state of preservation compared to ziggurats built and rebuilt piecemeal over centuries.
nodes.src: Roman Ghirshman, Chogha Zanbil excavations, on the ziggurat's construction technique.

nodes.label: Monumental bronze casting
nodes.full: Casting the roughly 1,750-kilogram Napirasu statue required lost-wax casting technique scaled far beyond ordinary metalwork, with a solid bronze exterior over a copper core — a technical achievement modern metallurgists still study for what it reveals about Elamite furnace capacity and casting control.
nodes.src: Statue of Napirasu, Louvre Sb 2731; technical analysis of its casting method.

nodes.label: Statue of Napirasu
nodes.full: Cast in bronze and copper at a weight of roughly 1,750 kilograms, the statue of Queen Napirasu — Untash-Napirisha's wife — is among the largest and technically most accomplished metal castings to survive from the entire ancient Near East, evidence of a bronze-working capacity matching the kingdom's most ambitious architectural projects.
nodes.src: Statue of Napirasu, Louvre Sb 2731.

nodes.label: Queen Napirasu remembered
nodes.full: Very few royal women anywhere in the ancient Near East were commemorated with an individually named, monumental statue in their own right rather than as an anonymous figure in a king's own inscriptions — Napirasu's bronze likeness, inscribed with her own name and titles, is a rare and deliberate exception.
nodes.src: Statue of Napirasu, Louvre Sb 2731, inscribed with her own dedicatory text.

nodes.label: Shutruk-Nahhunte
nodes.full: Shutruk-Nahhunte founded the dynasty that brought Elam to its greatest military power, campaigning repeatedly into Babylonia before his culminating 1158 BC conquest ended the four-century-old Kassite dynasty outright and carried its most celebrated monuments back to Susa as war trophies.
nodes.src: Shutruk-Nahhunte's own inscriptions on the captured Hammurabi and Naram-Sin monuments, Louvre.

nodes.label: Sack of Babylon
nodes.full: Shutruk-Nahhunte's decisive campaign against the last Kassite king, Enlil-nadin-ahi, ended the Kassite dynasty's roughly four-century rule over Babylon outright — the Elamite king carried off the Code of Hammurabi stele and the Victory Stele of Naram-Sin among his trophies, both later excavated at Susa and now among the Louvre's most famous holdings.
nodes.src: Elamite chronographic sources on the fall of the Kassite dynasty; the recovered monuments' own find-context at Susa.

nodes.label: Trophies at Susa
nodes.full: Shutruk-Nahhunte had his own triumphal inscription carved directly onto the captured Naram-Sin Victory Stele and the Code of Hammurabi, physically inscribing his conquest onto Mesopotamia's own most celebrated monuments — an act of deliberate cultural appropriation that ironically ensured both objects' survival for archaeologists to recover three thousand years later.
nodes.src: Naram-Sin Victory Stele and Code of Hammurabi stele, both Louvre, both carrying Shutruk-Nahhunte's added inscription.

nodes.label: Trophies from Babylon
nodes.full: The forced relocation of Babylon's most prestigious monuments to Susa — coerced rather than voluntary, but a genuine transmission of material culture across a political boundary nonetheless — is precisely how these objects came to be excavated in Iran rather than Iraq, reshaping where and how later archaeologists would encounter them.
nodes.src: Naram-Sin Victory Stele and Code of Hammurabi stele, both Louvre, both found at Susa rather than in Mesopotamia.

nodes.label: War booty as revenue
nodes.full: Beyond the celebrated monuments, Shutruk-Nahhunte's sack of Babylon brought back massive quantities of precious metal, temple treasure and portable wealth — plunder that functioned as a direct, one-time transfer of accumulated Mesopotamian wealth into the Elamite royal treasury.
nodes.src: Comparative Near Eastern evidence for the economic function of royal military plunder.

nodes.label: Deportations from Babylon
nodes.full: Following standard ancient Near Eastern practice for a conquered capital, Elamite forces likely deported skilled craftspeople and administrative personnel from Babylon alongside the physical plunder, though the textual record documents the objects taken far more explicitly than it does the people.
nodes.src: Comparative ancient Near Eastern practice for post-conquest deportation of skilled populations.

nodes.label: Elam at its zenith
nodes.full: With the Kassite dynasty destroyed and Babylon's most prestigious monuments displayed at Susa, Shutruk-Nahhunte's Elam stood at the height of its power and prestige in the Bronze Age Near East — a peak the kingdom would never again reach in its long subsequent history.
nodes.src: Comparative Bronze Age political history, on Elam's regional standing at its height.

nodes.label: Client king in Babylon
nodes.full: Following the conquest, Kutir-Nahhunte briefly installed his own son as a client ruler over Babylon — an attempt at direct Elamite political control over Mesopotamia's most prestigious throne that native Babylonian resistance would not tolerate for long.
nodes.src: Babylonian King List evidence for the brief Elamite-installed rulers of this interval.

nodes.label: Kutir-Nahhunte and Shilhak-Inshushinak
nodes.full: Kutir-Nahhunte briefly installed his own son on the Babylonian throne after his father's conquest, while his successor Shilhak-Inshushinak — the most prolific royal builder in Elamite history — left inscriptions recording the restoration or construction of well over a hundred temples across the kingdom during Elam's final and greatest flowering before its sudden collapse.
nodes.src: Shilhak-Inshushinak's building inscriptions, Susa; the scale of the corpus is itself the primary evidence for his reign's building program.

nodes.label: Inscribed record of rule
nodes.full: Shilhak-Inshushinak's inscriptions systematically catalogue his own building and restoration projects across dozens of named towns and temples — an administrative habit of comprehensive self-documentation that has made his reign, ironically, one of the best-attested in all of Elamite history precisely because of his taste for record-keeping.
nodes.src: Shilhak-Inshushinak building inscription corpus, Susa.

nodes.label: Inscriptions as history
nodes.full: Because no independent Elamite chronicle tradition of the Mesopotamian kind survives, Shilhak-Inshushinak's own extensive building and campaign inscriptions function as the closest thing to a connected historical narrative for the late Middle Elamite period — a king's self-commemoration serving, by accident of survival, as an entire era's primary historical source.
nodes.src: Shilhak-Inshushinak building and campaign inscription corpus, Susa.

nodes.label: Sit Shamshi ritual model
nodes.full: A bronze model depicting two nude figures performing a ritual before a sunrise, inscribed with Shilhak-Inshushinak's own dedication, offers a uniquely concrete visual record of an actual Elamite religious ceremony — rare physical evidence of ritual practice rather than only textual reference to a god's name.
nodes.src: Sit Shamshi bronze, Louvre Sb 2743.

nodes.label: Nebuchadnezzar I invades
nodes.full: After an initial failed attempt, the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar I invaded Elam in a punishing midsummer campaign, decisively defeated the Elamite army, and recovered the cult statue of Marduk that had been carried off to Susa decades earlier — reversing Shutruk-Nahhunte's triumph and inaugurating a long period of Elamite political eclipse.
nodes.src: The 'Marduk Prophecy' and Nebuchadnezzar I's own inscriptions on the Elamite campaign and Marduk's return.

nodes.label: Sudden reversal
nodes.full: Nebuchadnezzar I's decisive victory and the recovery of Marduk's statue plunged Elam into a long political eclipse from which no strong central Elamite kingship is well attested for nearly four centuries — the abruptness of the fall, following so closely on the zenith, is itself one of the more striking reversals in the whole Bronze Age Near East.
nodes.src: The 'Marduk Prophecy'; the near-total absence of Elamite royal inscriptions for the following centuries.

nodes.label: Kassite Babylon
nodes.full: The Kassite dynasty ruling Babylon is the dynastic partner with whom Elam’s kings cultivated marriage ties and the later target of the conquest of 1158 BC.
nodes.src: background — see the Babylon 1595–1155 BC folio
